subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The
issue that we are debating here behind all the talk is one thing, that is, interest rates. One can call it barren economic policies. This motion does. Basically, the sin that we are discussing is the fact that the government has been following a practice, which the previous government and the government before that followed, of accepting advice on economic, monetary and fiscal policy based on a type of approach that has been proven quantitatively wrong over the last 20 or 30 years.
In their last major national conference in Montreal, economists admitted they did not know and could not explain where they had been. They admitted they did not know where they were or where they were going. If economists could have admitted their complete failure to understand the system on which the world is working, I would think it behooves us in Parliament to be a little humble and accept the fact that neither do our advisers in Ottawa, our capital, know where they are. I use that as a starting point.
We have had a good demonstration today of the words "barren economic policies". I am sorry that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) left because I was going to make a comment or two. I sat with the minister when he was in the opposition. In that short period of government, I was happy to be on the government side in a committee where most of us in all parties agreed, that the ordinary members of Parliament had to take over from the cabinet and the ministers on the grounds that they had accepted this fallacious economic theory of the bank governor and the Department of Finance. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was loud and outspoken in his acceptance of the fact that the advice we were getting from the bank was wrong. He was outspoken in his acceptance of the fact that the advice we were getting from the government was wrong because it came from the same source. The hon. member now sits as a minister. He said it is all right to pay 20 per cent interest because the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) had said that the people of Canada are so wealthy that they can afford it. Last week the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in this House that the ordinary people of Canada are 50 per cent better off than they were ten years ago. Everyone thought that must mean that the government is doing a wonderful job.
I will not go over that barren ground of statistical statement which reached the point a number of years ago that the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board-who is no longer in this House-wrote a report to prove, on the basis of figures supplied by the then Bureau of Statistics, that the farmer was never wealthier than he was five or six years ago. I do not have to say what has happened to him; brilliant as he

May 22, 1981
Canadian Economy
was, he was wiped out in a western riding because of such stupidity.
We have seen the same stupidity in this House in the last week when not only the Minister of Finance mouthed this type of empty rhetoric, but the statement was repeated again today over and over again-that if we do not keep interest rates high, our dollar value will decline. There is no evidence that such a thing will happen.
In late 1979, when the governor of the Bank of Canada was asked for evidence that since he applied this monetary policy in 1975 it had kept the dollar value up, he said that he did not have any evidence. That made headlines in the newspapers. You would think reasonably literate people would not repeat that simple statement again, yet it happens half a dozen times a day in this House. People claim that if we do not keep interest rates high, our dollar will drop. The governor of the Bank of Canada or anyone else who looks at the evidence knows that there is no evidence of that; in fact, the evidence is to the contrary.
It is the same with the other great truth that they enunciate-that when you save a lot of money, interest rates are supposed to go down. Ten years ago Canada not only led the world in per capita savings, but between 1975 and 1979 the rate of savings increased from 5 per cent to 11 per cent; last year it dropped to 10 per cent. No other nation in the world saves more than Canada but the book on economics says that if savings are accumulated, interest rates are supposed to go down. I will not get into the semantics of that today, Mr. Speaker.
I hope that the government recognizes that in 1979 people sense that it was tired and bankrupt of ideas. That is why it was turfed out exactly two years ago today. Through an accident of political demagoguery and trickery it was returned and it thought that God had spoken-that it is now right in everything. We now see this tame, tired, dispirited group without ideas. It knows full well that the civil service cannot help it any more. The men at the top of the civil service have made up their minds about what is right, based on theories learned 30 or 40 years ago. In spite of all the quantitative evidence to show that they are wrong, they cannot bring themselves to make changes. For ministers of the Crown to defend that nonsense brings us all into disrepute.
A few years ago, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was so much against high interest rates that he said if the government did not bring them down, he would resign. He has destroyed his credibility because he did not resign. Now he comes into this House and reads off a list of things which is barren of ideas for helping out with the interest rate problem.
What we have to do today, Mr. Speaker, is to recognize that politics has fallen to the level of the scam or, to use an old fashioned word, fraud. The whole constitutional debate has been fraudulent. We have not even begun to discuss the Constitution. What we have seen is great posturing on the part of politicians as if they were examining something. The government must know that it has failed in that undertaking. It is
just a matter of letting it die a natural death. Then there is the great cry over energy prices. The government must accept the fact that it has failed and that it must make an agreement. But today, when the government is in trouble, the only solution known to civil servants is reorganization.
The Minister of Finance has become head of the policy group of the International Monetary Fund. That has happened to Canadians before and I am not opposed to it. Personally, I am glad he is out of the country so that he does not make us all look so foolish by making statements in the House. He has been zigging when he should have been zagging so often in the last eight or nine months, that it is a good thing he is out of the country! Let these newly evolving nations have him. If they think they will get anything out of him, they are mistaken.
I should like to put forward a few ideas that could have some possible positive effects, and I shall list them. There is no doubt in my mind that in the next two or three months, since we are not doing well in economics and since the constitutional scam has collapsed, as has the scam over energy prices-even Ontario betrayed it the other day-there will have to be a new scam. It will be Canada taking a position among these newly developing nations as the great white father who is on their side.
Let us be honest, Mr. Speaker. We want to help the developing nations in the world. Let us not try to hide what is actually happening, however. We know that they will not be helped by a continuation of the present type of handout. These handouts have done more to make enemies for the United States, Canada, Great Britain, France, Germany, and the other nations that gave them handouts. These newly developing nations know that a handout is given primarily for the purpose of lining the pockets of the local politicians of the governing party.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Those countries know that the pockets of Canadians are also being lined because not a single handout is given unless the nations buy something in Canada.
As many hon. members may know, I have felt a load on my conscience over the last 20-odd years about doing something about this. As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and others well know, I have been trying to organize international trading companies which would help these underdeveloped countries trade with others. They would make money in the process and so could afford to buy what they want, where they want. It would be a three-way trade, not this bilateral economic imperialism that we have practised under the present handout policy.
I know what ministers and what ordinary businessmen in these countries say. They say, "Your country comes to us with all these offers and a list of things that we are expected to buy from Canada." They know that it is economic blackmail. They may smile at you so as to get some more handouts but in their hearts they hate your guts. That is the frank truth of the handout route.
May 22, 1981

I have never met a more dedicated group of civil servants then those in CIDA. Yet I know what they must endure to go through all these monkeyshines. When one country gives to another country, you cannot really enforce the carrying out of that program in the other country.
What is a better way of doing it? I have mentioned the International Trading Congress. I think I have said enough about it. Their programs are working at no cost to government. Both sides benefit and world trade has improved.
I think hon. members probably know that in 1961 the People's Republic of China had only $400 million a year in trade, $200 million going to Russia and $200 million coming back to China. What is it today? They have $30 billion a year in trade. That has been done by free trading institutions moving in and out, sometimes to government, but more often just private businessmen going back and forth and dealing with corporations. Handouts are just a new form of imperialism. These people out there know it, and so do we. They are ashamed. I am not going into the question of the competence of handling these programs. We should not be giving them handouts. We should give them lower interest rates, if they take aid in the form of loans. They have no more chance of paying back a loan at low interest rates than they have with a high interest rate loan if the loan is not properly utilized to produce more wealth with which to pay it back. I do not want to spend too much time on that aspect either.
The last type of rap we have had over the last ten years started with Malta. Someone came along with this great Christian concept that we should turn the wealth of the oceans over to the newly developing nations. My God, wouldn't our fellow men think we are wonderful people? The ocean wealth is the heritage of mankind. Every nitwit in every political party in Canada is in fraud and scam from the word go right up to their necks. The wealth at the bottom of the sea under international law belongs to the coastal states, as far as they can develop it. With present technology, that means everywhere. Six sevenths of the world is ocean today under sovereign control by international law of the coastal states. Canada owns the resources halfway across the Atlantic, the Arctic and the Pacific. That is the international law. Yet civil servants who come into our political parties never even mention that the international law still applies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: How much of the high seas?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The high seas have nothing to do with the bottom of the sea convention, if the hon. member knows anything about it.
I want to make it very clear that Canada put forward that proposal in 1958. It was unanimously approved in committee at the Law of the Sea Convention, unanimously approved at the United Nations in 1962, and enough nations ratified the proposal to make it international law, and there it remains.
Why should nitwits in our political parties here in Canada play a part in this scam of pretending that we are going to give
Canadian Economy
something from the bottom of the sea to these new nations? At present we can do it very easily by simply granting them a certain royalty, 5 per cent, 7 per cent, 8 per cent, or whatever we agree upon. If we want to give them a handout, 7 per cent of the gross might be acceptable. There is no way to ever get these nations to agree on the split. We would have to turn it over to a United Nations body, such as the International Monetary Fund or the World Bank. With their programs, it would probably be more rationally assigned.
I have mentioned three or four different types of scams: the handouts, the low interest rate scam and the scam of pretending that we are helping people when we are really trying to delude them. The newest one I have mentioned is the one where Canada will take the lead with the wealthy nations of the world toward a better North-South relationship.
We all know what that is. The Prime Minister has made up his mind what he is going to do. He wants to go out with something good. He has failed with every other thing. He has failed on his constitutional gambits. He has failed on his energy gambits. He is not able to do anything on the economic side, so he has to pretend that he is leading the world to higher and better things. Whenever you try to persuade nations such as Britain, France, Germany, Japan and the United States to join together in a helpful procedure for the newly developing nations, boy, that is real pretence. There is only one way you get things through these countries sensibly and that is to help them make more money first so they can do without the handouts.
The proposals I want to put forward all have precedents. When Malayasia wanted a handout to fight communism in 1958, what we did was to clear the land in ten acre jungle lots, plant red rubber trees and pay the people directly wages of $70 a month. When the rubber trees came into production and they were able to pay for running their operations and looking after their families, we asked, as Canadians, for a 15 per cent return. We were paid back in three years.
If we can do this type of thing for Malayasia without getting rid of interest rates, and stop communist insurgency by letting people own their land, they will never become communist. Why can we not use the same rules for Canadians?
Canada took the lead in 1959 and then in 1961 on another project. Instead of handouts, we set up an international program through the United Nations called the world food program, under which were not authorized handouts except in cases of famine or emergency. Today we are beginning the twentieth year of that program. There is no program in the whole of the United Nations working more successfully and achieving more good than this one. Ninety per cent of the billions of dollars we have raised and given to this program has been spent in constructive enterprises, and only 10 per cent has gone to handouts for emergencies. There are precedents to do things in a constructive way so that everyone benefits.
Because my time has just about run out, I want to plead with this Parliament to start putting proposals forward in the hope that in its desperation the government will accept a few of these precedents and begin to apply this type of construe-

May 22, 1981
Canadian Economy
tiveness, aimed not only at our own economic problems but to realize that we will help ourselves if we help the other fellow first.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada today is in a crisis of confusion. We are squandering our government resources, our people resources, our natural resources and our intellectual resources. We are even in the process of squandering a heritage of freedom by destroying a process of common law and a parliamentary form of government that has at least protected our liberty and freedom down through the ages when other forms have failed.
In the past, all emerging and growing societies have given priority to their economies, for it is only with a disciplined, well-managed economic base that the material needs and social wants of man can be provided. Surely the lessons of the Soviet bloc countries, with their state-owned and controlled economies, massive police forces and armies, are there as warnings to us. Surely the economic crises of the welfare states that the NDP have been giving to us as examples of what they would like to see in Canada are a warning that we should not ignore.
Today in Canada we have a gang of socialists marauding under the cloak of the Liberal Party of Canada, repeating the mistakes of the past and of contemporary history. One can only conclude that the screwed up priorities, the mismanagement of this country's economy, the squandering of our resources is deliberate, with the intent of removing any sense of freedom and incentive from our economy, all in the name of an egalitarian welfare state where men will live under a totally structured economy.
Man was not born equal, and in egalitarian societies where men are forced to live as equals, they are not free. When we lose the essential elements of a free economy, as we are doing in Canada today, we lose the basic foundation of our freedom. With the continual emphasis on structure rather than behaviour in the legislation that is being tabled in this House by this government, we are chopping down the tree that feeds the roots of our freedom and of a free economy.
I do not believe that this drift to economic and social oblivion has to be inevitable. We should turn our considerable talents and energies to the many alternatives that are available to us. First, we should take advantage of the lessons of history that are in the Laffer curve and we should deliver fiscal politics that will once again spark the energy, ingenuity and talent that is now lying dormant within our Canadian people. It is the collective attitude of the nation's people which is the ingredient that builds or destroys a nation. We should manage our future, which means forward planning. Herein I agree with the NDP. It means forward planning and budgeting of our people and our resources. However, what do we have today?
Today the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) stood up here and gave to us his industrial strategy
which was just a tangled web of microprograms and activities within one department. In no way can we deliver ourselves today from our microproblems. What this country needs is sound, fundamental fiscal policies. History tells us what we must do. History is pleading with us not to repeat the mistakes of the past. What is our Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) doing in Gabon when the great national crisis of today could be solved with a sound fundamental fiscal policy? He should be here preparing his budget for October.
Today we have deliberately delayed the many megaprojects that could deliver this country to energy self-sufficiency by the year 1990. What are we going to do with this delay? If we could reach energy self-sufficiency by 1990, that would be the greatest gift we could give to the Third World, removing our international demands for energy from the rest of the world. If we could look after our own needs at home, that energy would be available for others. Here we have tied up all of these megaprojects and are backing them up behind a dam. It is my guess that this government is going to let them all go at once, creating the most massive shortage of trades people, the most massive shortage of labour, shortage of steel, shortage of transportation, and I do not see one shred of planning in the delivery of the great opportunities that are ahead of us in this country. Not one shred of planning did I hear about today from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
We in this country are critically short of tradespeople and people with trade skills. This country historically has been drawing them from the countries and schools of Europe. Whenever we needed them, we brought them over on immigration programs. Today those countries need those skilled tradespeople themselves so they are not available to us. We have known this crisis has been coming for the last decade, but where have we put in place educational programs to deliver the trade and skill needs that this country requires in time for the demand that is shortly ahead of us if we ever are going to get these megaprojects under way? Can you imagine what $1.2 billion spent in trade education would do for this country and the Third World instead of a string of broken down gas stations across this country?
My colleague, the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) pointed out that a co-ordinated approach was in place in the United States to deal with the inflationary pressures within that country. It is important, in addition to recognizing the co-ordinated approach in the United States, to recognize that we need something more for our basic economic structure which, although once similar to the United States, is no longer so.
We have an additional challenge over and above the coordinated approach of the United States. For instance, in Canada we borrow on a short-term basis with floating interest rates that are at a crisis level, and I guess will keep going up until we have strangled all the discretionary spending there is out of our economy.
Homes that should be financed on a 20-year basis are now on a one-year and five-year term, with interest incentives that have kept people rolling them over on a year to year basis,
May 22, 1981

thinking, hoping and praying that interest rates will drop. Only short term and demand money is available to the small and medium-size enterprise sector of Canada, with terrible pressure being exerted on any attempt to improve productivity in those sectors.
In the United States, on the other hand, long-term money at lower interest rates is available for long-term purposes, such as new and more productive plants and new productive capacity. We do not have that edge available to us in Canada, particularly for the small and medium-enterprise sector. In this area, our financial structure is different and it should not, in my opinion, be blindly following the interest rate monetarist lead of the United States. We have a different need entirely.
For over three years there has been an initiative for long, low, long-term interest rates on the bureaucratic merry-go-round between the Department of Finance, and the Department of Insurance and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Powerful establishment interests have all but smothered this private sector initiative that would loosen up all the savings my colleague from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) was talking about that are now dammed up in the pension funds, RRSPs and tax shelters of Canada. All those funds need is a covenant of guarantee in order to be released on a 20 and even 30-year-term basis at 0.3 and 0.4 points under prime.
In July 1980 I asked the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce what he was doing to get this initiative out of the tangled web of bureaucracy of the federal government. I remind you it has been there for some three years. That initiative has been denied to the private sector of Canada. This is something that members on both sides of the House should be concerned about and should address.
We have examples of banks lending long-term money in Canada to specified projects at rates well below prime and on a long-term basis. If banks have surplus funds to lend on a preferred long-term basis to some projects, why do we not examine why that is and why it is not available to other good, solid, secure activities in the Canadian market? Why are we so selective? That is the question I ask. The interest rate problem in Canada has and is aggravating our productivity factor. Both the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance know that the only way we can climb out of this national, even world, dilemma is by improving our productivity. Yet the interest rate policies of this government are deliberately working against that important need.
Our productivity in the last year has dropped 1.4 per cent. Some of us in this House do not even understand what productivity is, for I heard the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) needling my colleague, the hon. member for York-Peel, regarding the pride shown in having created 300,000 new jobs in Canada. Not one of those jobs is in an area which creates wealth. It is only jobs which are in the process of adding to the value of goods that can carry the payrolls of those not involved in that economic process. In other words,
Canadian Economy
300,000	jobs are not productive jobs; the same work and goods could be produced in Canada with 300,000 fewer people. That is the burden that government policy is putting on those who do true-value work in this country.
There are games being played that I do not understand. For instance, the federal government is a dominant factor in issuing extendable bonds. They talk about their bonds bearing 16 per cent interest for three years. Those bonds now have an extension for a further ten years at a higher rate of interest. The budget will show the lower rate of interest as the cost of financing, but nowhere in the projections is it reflected what the higher cost down the road will be. These are half-truths and games which we do not need any more in this country if we are going to address the serious problems that should be dealt with on a truthful, factual and thinking basis.
The Minister of Finance and the Bank of Canada are correct in saying that higher interest rates can control inflation. As I said during question period today, it is correct to conclude that government policy is to squeeze the public until there is no discretionary spending left. We heard the Prime Minister's answer to my question today. He does not have the slightest bit of consideration for those people in this country who have put in their work, done their jobs, are in retirement but have absolutely no discretionary spending.
Today all Canadian business in the general stream of commerce is hooked on the short-term changing interest rates which create havoc with our productive capacity and costs, and benefit only the paper pushers and the banks. There is little if any reward left in Canada for those who create jobs and maintain payrolls. All the rewards go to the developers, the industrial landlords, the banks, the chartered accountants, the lawyers-the paper pushers. The guy who has to manage, has to balance things, has his guarantee on the line, risks his home and his lifetime of work, is almost at the point, if not at the point, of no return. There are very serious complications and a lack of incentive today for those capable of managing and creating productive units. In fact, in my opinion, this is rapidly becoming a national crisis.
Labour laws today allow secondary picketing.

speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
You bet they do, and there is an inability to adjust to production costs and to market realities with our swinging interest rates. All of these things are creating an impossible situation, even to the point where a non-productive and unsuitable person can hardly be removed from a payroll today.
This government refuses to give the job-creating sector tax points for research and development incentives. Their servants continue to insist that innovators come cap in hand to the bureaucrats who say yea or nay to these projects. Some of them have just too much pride, and most risk takers in the small and medium enterprise sector are just too busy to find the time for this cap-in-hand process. The rules of the game in business are being constantly changed and this damages any chance of improving productivity levels. Intervention in struc-

May 22, 1981
Canadian Economy
ture is the order of the day of this government. Only the oligopolies, the large multinational corporations and the large corporate entities, have the time, the resources and the payroll ability to play the game the government asks of the economic community. The SME sector is really out to lunch.
1 would like for a moment to turn to the NDP rump of the Liberal socialist party of Canada with its phony, negative whining that is motivated, in my opinion, by envy and bitterness, for its members have attacked every significant initiative in this country that is there and waiting to resolve our unemployment and energy problems.
They demand more and more of the system at large, but hinder the very process of providing the wealth needed to improve the social benefits of this welfare society. They mouth shallow platitudes to the small business sector when their masters are the big union bosses who are interested only in the maximum grab from the economy for a minority of the work force. They call for wealth distribution while living off the avails of big Liberal monopolies. In my opinion, members of the NDP speak with a political forked tongue.
Earlier I touched on the fact that our structure is different from that of the U.S., and I discussed the energy factor there. I have discussed the fact that the government is involved in extendable bonds which place an unfair burden and an advantage in the marketplace, and disturb and distort our interest rate structure. The government does not show the cost of the future rate and it takes an advantage away from other forces in the market which might want to attract that capital. In my opinion, these tricky games make it most difficult for the rest of the business community to have a fair share and a place.
This policy is leading to a reduction in wealth and a destruction of the Canadian dream. It can only lead to state control of our economy. When that happens, when that day comes, I suggest that anybody hearing this plea in this chasm should understand that their very basic freedoms are threatened. There is no answer to be found in a welfare state and Sweden is an example of it. We are falling into the same economic trap and dilemma they have already developed for themselves. Please, can we not learn from this?
One thing we might do which would resolve our interest rate problem, our low Canadian dollar problem and our productivity problem would be to seriously study putting between $50 billion and $70 billion into our international monetary fund as a reserve. In that way our interest rates would come down, our dollar value would go up and our cost of living would come down.
One might say that is a lot of money. I tell you it is a pittance compared to what the present policy has robbed from the pension funds, the savings plans and the savings of individuals throughout Canada. I would urge the government to perhaps seek co-operation from this side in taking a very serious look at the delivery of a good, sizeable and usable reserve which would give stability to our interest rates and our international exchange rates.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking in favour of this motion today. The last sentence asks the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to introduce a budget with corrective measures before July 1 or resign. I fully support that.
Our present Minister of Finance has been in Liberal cabinets longer than any of his colleagues, so he is actually more responsible than they for blank-cheque government. He was there, right at the start, for the introduction of blank-cheque government, uncontrolled spending and changing the rules so that there is no longer parliamentary control over expenditures. After listening to some of the Liberals speak today, I suggest they spend a little more time reading the report of the Auditor General and the report of the Lambert commission on how this Liberal government has been running the country and controlling expenditures. Perhaps the term "cutback" is not correct. It really should be eliminating waste and mismanagement within government, and there has been no attempt by this government to get together with the provinces to eliminate duplication and to try to find ways and means to improve control over our expenditures.
There are many examples around us. For example, on the Campeau project over in Hull there was an over-expenditure of $300 million. That is just one little example. Another one comes to mind; the UIC fraud squad was disbanded a number of years ago because the things that squad was coming up with were embarrassing to the Liberal government. That squad was disbanded. It would have exposed fraud costing about $100 million a year. Hon. members opposite did not impress me at all with any of the speeches they made this afternoon.
I am going to speak about some of the untruths of hon. members opposite and point out once again that their word means absolutely nothing. That is old hat, but I will refer to just a couple of points. The Liberals were going to hold increases in government spending under the growth of the gross national product. They have absolutely no intention of doing any such thing. There was to be an industrial strategy, job creation and increased Canadian ownership. Canadian ownership has just been increased through the purchase of Petrofina and by sending $1 billion to Belgium and $1 million to a Swiss bank to pay for the transaction.
My friend, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), spoke about establishing a fund to help small businesses facing high interest rates. Just imagine if that $1 billion had been put to that use instead of being sent into the Belgian economy!
Prior to the last election, the Liberals stated that they would achieve energy security at a fair price. I will go into some detail on that in a moment. That statement is absolute nonsense. There was the promise that gas increases would be kept below 18 cents a gallon, and we now find that the price is increasing as much as 60 cents a gallon. That is another broken promise. The Liberals promised to ensure prosperity through economic growth in every region. Then they introduced the NEP, which is killing economic growth in Canada.
May 22, 1981

The Liberals promised to help first those who need assistance. I am our spokesman on veterans' pensions, and I know the problems of veterans respecting the length of time it takes to process applications and the problems the widows of veterans are having. I know the serious problems rail pensioners are having. This government is doing absolutely nothing about those problems.
These problems have been with us for years, and this government refuses to deal with them. Some rail pensioners receive increases of $4 a year. We get the runaround from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), who say they will help those who need assistance.
This is not the only government in the world which has not controlled expenditures or seen that money is spent properly. Almost every government in the world is the same in this respect. There have been only four since 1948 which have operated in a responsible manner. The government with the best record of all was the Diefenbaker government between 1957 and 1963. That government was not a blank-cheque government. It was composed of a group of responsible men who saw that we received proper value for our tax dollars, and the inflation rate was held to 1.2 per cent. When the Liberals came into power in 1963, they took the lid off. Mr. Pearson was going to be a big, tough prime minister with respect to a dock workers strike. He was going to show them. He gave the dock workers a huge increase instead of giving them a guarantee of job security which they wanted. Anyone can look at a graph and see that that is when spending took off, and it has never stopped.
This afternoon I picked up an article in The Toronto Sun.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Our country is in a disgraceful situation. This article quotes statistics. The Liberals are laughing. They do not like any newspaper which continually exposes this fraudulent government and its mismanagement. The article reads in part as follows:
Metro's eviction rate is soaring and sheriffs offices face hotted-up hostility in their struggle to keep abreast of the growing workload.
Evictions to April 30 are up 10 per cent over last year, when the rate jumped 28.5 per cent from 1979.
I say to the two laughing frontbenchers opposite that that means that thousands of Canadians are being evicted from their homes. When we were in government, we introduced a mortgage credit plan for home owners which would have assisted them greatly, and we would not have had as many evictions today. However, the New Democratic Party and the Liberals were violently opposed to any assistance for home owners. The article goes on to say the following:
Over all, evictions of residential and commercial tenants and evictions resulting from foreclosed mortgages have risen an awesome 23 per cent from the 971 recorded in 1976, the year after Ontario's rent controls were introduced.
Boris Kashuba, deputy sheriff in charge of evictions for York district, yesterday said his eight men are encountering "a more hostile, militant mood" from the public.
Canadian Economy
I guess they are, with these disgraceful interest rates this government is supposed to be reducing. I remember the slick Liberal television commercials during the last election campaign. They were going to reduce high interest rates. Of course, they had absolutely no intention of doing any such thing. This article goes on to say the following:
There were 3,279 evictions last year in Metro compared to 2,550 in 1979.
The sheriffs people are going into suburban areas because of foreclosures on homes whose owners have given up the battle to meet mortgage payments. The article goes on:
Tenants faced with rental arrears are borrowing the money to keep their landlords satisfied because they fear they won't be able to find alternative accommodation.
That is a national disgrace in a country like Canada. It is a national disgrace that people are being booted out of their homes right and left. The Liberal party lied in the last election campaign on television about its intention to lower interest rates. Now that they are in power, they do not do anything about this at all, and they have no intention of ever doing anything about it.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) made a ridiculous speech in Winnipeg a week or so ago. He pointed out that the National Energy Program is not primarily an employment program but that it will stimulate employment. What a ridiculous and untrue statement!
We have figures from the oil industry showing that the NEP will cost 60,000 jobs. More than 60,000 jobs may be lost by mid-summer due to the increasing number of oil and gas rigs leaving Canada, the Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors has stated. Stan Jones, the executive director of the association, has said that the 50 per cent decline in the number of rigs drilling for oil and gas during the past year has surpassed the worst predictions of that association. Jones blamed the federal government's National Energy Program and its failure to reach an oil pricing agreement with Alberta for creating the dramatic slump in the oil industry.
I do not know why they have not been able to reach an agreement. If I were involved in those negotiations, I would have no hesitation in paying Saskatchewan and Alberta $35 a barrel. I would rather pay them $35 a barrel than pay $50 a barrel to Mexico. Mexican oil is of poor quality. We have to add Canadian oil to bring it up to a proper standard. I would rather pay Alberta and Saskatchewan $35 a barrel than send $45 to the rich OPEC countries to make them richer. The ridiculous NEP does not make any sense at all.
Mr. Jones went on to say that the slowdown threatens to eliminate more than 60,000 jobs on the oil fields and across Canada by midsummer. "In little less than six months the National Energy Program has effectively dismantled more than half of the most dynamic industry in Canada," Jones said.
And that is what the Liberals call progress and creating jobs and self-sufficiency. We are not going to become self-sufficient at all. By 1990, under the government's program, we are going

May 22, 1981
Canadian Economy
to be sending $182 billion more out of the country to buy imported oil. We are only to be 55 per cent self-sufficient. Mr. Jones went on to say that there were 370 drilling rigs working in Canada last May compared with 177 this year, and that most of the rigs have been moved or auctioned off in the U.S.
I do not think the Liberals really understand whose economy they are trying to help. They have certainly been of welcome assistance to the United States.
Here is a great article out of Denver, Colorado. It reads:
Many Canadian based oil companies are setting up operations in the United States because of higher profits.
Profit is not a dirty word in the United States but this government, under its policy of cutting down the cash flow of these small Canadian firms, is making it impossible for them to exist, and that is why they are getting out of this country. The article goes on:
Oil industry sources say that in the last year, more than 100 Canadian companies, mostly from Calgary and Edmonton with a few from Vancouver and Toronto, have established or are planning to establish U.S. offices.
For many of these Canadian companies, the Rocky Mountain states are their first choice.
About 80 of the 100 companies represented at a recent energy conference in Denver were based in Canada, says Dave Lytle, a Canadian oilman recently transferred from Edmonton.
Canadian oil company executives here say they can make up to 10 times more profit from a U.S. oil well.
And when they are making lots of profits they are spending more, paying the shareholders more, and Liberals from Ontario and Quebec had better do a little close checking too of how it is affecting them because from 42 cents to 47 cents of every dollar spent in the oil industry is spent in Ontario, so they are really going to get walloped very sharply, probably in the Sarnia area. The article goes on:
By contrast, they say U.S. oilmen are praising president Reagan. U.S. drilling and new petroleum discovery rates are at a record high and U.S. oil imports have dropped to their lowest level since 1975.
And what are we doing? We are importing more oil under this ridiculous National Energy Program. There is $500,000 an hour leaving this country for Mexico, Venezuela and the OPEC countries to import oil, but the government will not sit down and make a sensible agreement with Alberta and Saskatchewan. Reading further, it is stated that:
U.S. oilmen welcome the arrival of the Canadians although some of them are unhappy with Ottawa's Canadianization policies.
"We need the drilling rigs, the exploration capital and Canadian expertise," says one U.S. oilman.
Well, they can thank the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Labour, the cabinet and all the rest of them for assisting the United States economy and helping the United States to achieve self-sufficiency.
I mentioned earlier the Liberal promises to look after the underprivileged and all the rest. I am glad that the Minister of Labour is here today because we have had one exchange on what is going to happen to the rail pensioners in Canada. There seems to be considerable confusion between the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour as to who is responsible for showing some leadership in assisting these
people who have really been getting the runaround. A lot of people get the runaround from government. In many cases it is not intentional, but in this case it has gone beyond any reasonable explanation and somebody is going to have to take the initiative. I hope the Minister of Labour will do so. I would just quote to him what some of these pensioners are receiving. Some receive $115 a month, others receive $178, $212, or $224 a month, and they have been trying for years to get a few dollars more and some kind of indexing system.
The Minister of Labour has written letters to different unions to say that he has the matter under study, that he recognizes there is a problem and he is going to be doing something about it. That is what it sounds like in his letters, but when I asked him yesterday in the House about this, he started talking about the Hall report. Well, that report is about five or six years old, and the first of these letters that he wrote to the unions was in May of 1980 and nothing has been done since. They are supposed to be able to have the unions bargain for them, but they cannot because management will not recognize the unions as bargaining agents for the pensioners and we are just going around and around in a big circle. So I hope the minister is present at this committee on Tuesday morning so that we can discuss this in a little more detail, and I hope he will give me some kind of assurance that he will take a close look at this particular problem because it is a real problem. Those who have retired from about 1977 onwards are really not too badly off but prior to that the pensions they receive are absolutely ridiculous.
I just want to comment further on statements on interest rates by the Liberals when they were in opposition. These statements are just unbelievable, especially from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) who said he was going to do something about interest rates and that he would resign if they did not come down. In fact, they have gone up about eight points since he made that statement. And he pointed out:
-because of the harmful effects of high interest rates on consumers, businessmen, especially small businessmen, and the entire economy, there should be an urgent study by the finance committee, where the governor of the bank would come, and the minister of finance-
Well, when we were in government, we established such a committee and they were only half way through their work when we were defeated in the House of Commons by a motion presented by the NDP saying nothing was being done about interest rates. And at that time the Governor of the Bank of Canada was one of the next witnesses to appear.
This is the sort of thing you get from the NDP. One of their spokesmen today was criticising our motion. They have a lot of nerve criticizing our motion or anything we do considering the devious manner in which they operate in and out of the House of Commons. We could very well have found a number of solutions to this problem had that committee been allowed to carry on, and we have asked repeatedly that it be established once again, but the Liberals refused to do anything about it. They have made their point perfectly clear: we are going to have to live with this interest rate problem because they have no intention of doing anything about it. They will tell you they
May 22, 1981

are going to do something about it during an election but once they get in, that is the finish.
Then this great Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce went on to say to the Minister of Finance:
Mr. Minister, I want to point out to you that your high interest rate policy would slow down the economy: it will mean the loss of thousands of jobs; it will mean increases in the cost of living. It will probably bring the housing and construction industry to a halt, with thousands of jobs being lost in those sectors.
Well, what is he doing about it? He is not doing anything at all.
I see I have one minute left, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure this debate will be brought to a dramatic conclusion by one of the better debaters in the House of Commons, namely, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was wondering whether we had found a new speaker on the floor who was announcing the next speaker in this debate. However, this is a very serious motion we have before us today and I would just like to remind everyone of the following words in the motion:
That this House condemns the government's barren economic policies, which are destroying the stability, productivity and competitiveness of the Canadian economy;
That is the first element, and it is a threefold element. The motion terminates by urging the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to introduce a budget with corrective measures before July 1, 1981, or resign.
I suspect the Minister of Finance would be unable to devise the required corrective measures, unless he examined more closely the National Energy Program announced with his previous budget. It was really the pith and substance of the budget, since the budget itself contained very little of a budgetary nature.
What distresses me most in the present circumstances is the unthinking manner in which the government makes use of our national resources, on the grounds that it knows better how to dispose of the national wealth than those who earn it. The wages of wanton extravagance designed to buy voter support are the economic dilemma in which we find ourselves today. Rather than designing an intelligent program to make the country a worthy legacy for generations to come, the government embarked upon a short-term desire to maintain itself in power. It uses the hard-earned wealth of taxpayers to buy their support. I consider it tragic, pitiful, distressing, shameful and verging on treasonous and treacherous for a government to abuse the mandate granted to it in January, 1980.
Our resource base is almost limitless. What policies do we see the government creating to develop the resource base so that we could hand over a flourishing economy to those generations to follow? I could think of two or three examples, but one of the most fabulous-and I use that word in its real meaning-is the coal resources of the Rocky Mountains. Of course, the tar sands and heavy oils are other examples. The
Canadian Economy
government is doing everything to destroy initiative and to prevent the accumulation of individual initiative to bring those resources on stream.
The government believes it can do it better. How does it go about it? It charges Canadians who drive automobiles an extra .8 of a cent per litre or 3.5 cents per gallon in order to buy an enterprise and send SI.5 billion of motorists' funds out of the country. Those who heat by oil, find their heating costs have risen by the same amount. This is being done to acquire an enterprise based offshore, not to produce more energy. It is only to obtain ownership of a resource which has already been found by somebody else. Why is that $1.5 billion not being used to take us closer to energy self-sufficiency?
The government refuses or is possibly incapable of devising a program which meets the legitimate needs of the provinces with resources and at the same time the legitimate need of the central authority for funds for other purposes. It is really the destruction of individual initiative which I deplore so much. No one in the world, certainly no upstanding Canadian, would regret the effort the government has taken to look after the needy, but why must the government look after those who are not in need? There is no need to destroy initiative by robbing Canadians to meet needs which do not exist. We are all prepared to share what we have in order to help those who are unfortunate, but I see no point in contributing a cent to a pension for an E. P. Taylor or even a pension for myself. 1 am prepared to stand on my own feet. I have had good fortune. I have experienced good health throughout my life and hopefully have done an honourable day's work every day I worked, for which I was compensated. I have been able to look after myself and my future. Why should they rob from me to pay me after I can no longer work? This is stupid nonsense. We can help those people who were mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), those railroad pensioners who are in need. We are prepared to do that, but the government has overspent to the point of profligacy. I cannot think of a stronger word than that.
If time permits, I would like to cite a few figures and to offer a few ideas because the government has shown in its performance that it has none of its own except to tax and to invent nonsensical projects which do nothing for productivity. Every day the government boasts about the number of jobs it has created. It has not created jobs except those in the public service, and those it has created in plenty. I wonder what is the productivity of the public service at the present time. It used to be good. I say that with pride. I do not think it is as great as it was.
There has been no attempt to curb credit. The whole design of the government is to destroy the initiative of the individual to work and to invest.
If it is true, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been saying for these last two or three days when he has been attacked about the high interest rates, that there is more spending now than there ever was before, there is spending

May 22, 1981
Canadian Economy
now because of the uncertainties of the future. That is why. The uncertainty is causing this spending. There are surplus funds in people's pockets. There is no question about that. However, they are spending it wantonly. They are not saving or investing. They are not prepared to stand on their own feet because this government has destroyed that incentive which had inspired my father and mother.

speechtext: A point of order, Mr. Speaker. I was wondering if the hon. gentleman who has just made a statement relating to the inability of Canadians to save would address the phenomenon of Canadians saving at a rate which is twice that of the United States.

speechtext: That is not a point of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Good fact, though; interesting, isn't it?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: During the last three or four days we have been talking about inflation and interest rates. Bankruptcies are a tragedy. It is a family tragedy and an individual tragedy when a man who has put his heart and soul, his energy, and all his capital into a project finds that with the requirement to borrow further funds he is faced with insuperable charges and that therefore either his house has to go, his farm has to go, or his equipment has to go. Sometimes his wife even deserts him. That is also sad.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Save a lot of money that way!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Don't believe it!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The breakup of the family unit as a result of these stressful situations brought about by inflation which this government has done nothing to control, and excessive rates, makes me wonder why we should be so ready, under an enterprise known as the Export Development Corporation, the EDC, to provide favourable, advantageous rates of borrowing to foreign governments or companies provided that they spend those funds in this country. I think particularly of shipbuilding.
In a speech about two or three years ago, I mentioned the number of ships built for other countries. I think the figure was something like 30 in five years. They had been built for such countries as Poland, Argentina and France. I understand that a French ship was built not very long ago. Why are we lending these funds to foreign countries when we might just as easily lend them to our own citizens to build our own merchant marine? I just do not understand this. Notwithstanding its name, why should the EDC not provide these credits to Canadian citizens so that we might further their purposes within Canada?
Two days ago, on May 19, I was impressed when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) offered two or three suggestions as to what this government might do-

speechtext: We want Jarvis!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
-in a global manner to assist those who are in trouble because of the inflation or high
interest rates. When the Conservative government was in power, we, of course, did introduce those features in the mortgage interest deductibility plan and also on the energy side. For example, it put a stop to the requirement to pay the added tax which was to be imposed on heating oil. This government has done nothing like that. It seems as though suggestions which come from this side of the House are, ipso facto, untouchable. They should not even be examined.
One of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was to make governmental provision for loans at a reasonable rate on condition. For example, if the purpose of the loan were to buy a house, if that house were sold at a vast profit within two or three years, then the capital gain on the investment would be shared 50-50 with the government. I think that makes a good deal of sense.
I have one further suggestion to make, and it is not new. It was put in practice at a time which only a few people in this House can remember. I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would certainly remember it. I remember those days, too, as a teenager, when farms were being closed down and farmers were having to leave their land and go somewhere to find relief, the dough. It was a shameful time. I think there is still a lesson to be learned from that period which we might consider. In its briefest terms, it would consist of this: there would be a moratorium on the repayment of capital borrowing. The interest would be repayable. However, there would be a moratorium on capital borrowing. To my way of thinking, this would have two very important effects. It would mean that the money that was out would be earning its keep. The rent on it, even at 20 per cent, could be faced. On the other hand, the repayment of capital would be deferred and the life of the loan would be correspondingly extended at the far end until the interest rates had come down and a refinancing could be arranged.
Besides the advantage to the borrower, the other advantage is that it would take a great deal of capital out of circulation because as capital is returned to the lender, it would be loaned out again. However, if some of that capital could be withdrawn from circulation, then I think the effect on inflation would be catastrophic. The inflation rate would drop because the extent of capital available for borrowing would be reduced by an immeasurable amount. I cannot even conceive the amount.
The one thing which would have to be examined very carefully in putting forward this notion would be the bureaucracy required to examine cases of requests for the moratorium. As I say, it would have to be reviewed, for instance, every six months or every year so that advantage would not be taken of borrowers. The dual advantage of having the borrower able to pay something, to stand on his own feet, pay the interest, and at the same time withdraw capital from circulation would have a very important and depressive effect on the inflation rate. That is one suggestion I put out to the government for its consideration.
